title.value: Pd/Brønsted Acid Co-catalyzed Dehydrative Coupling of Propargylic Alcohols with Diarylphosphine Oxides

abstract.value: An efficient dehydrative coupling of propargylic alcohols with diarylphosphine oxides to construct tetrasubstituted allenylphosphoryl compounds in the presence of a Pd/Brønsted acid co-catalyst has been developed. As a benefit from the use of a Brønsted acid, this reaction could perform under mild conditions with excellent yields, accommodating a wide range of functional groups. The potential utility of this method has also been demonstrated. ![](../extracted/pd-brnsted-acid-co-catalyzed-dehydrative-coupling-of-propargylic-alcohols-with-diarylphosphine-oxides/images/09257d425579721a129218253eaa528445b42bd1569ffbccc1c11fc0fe6739d6.jpg) <details> <summary>chemical</summary> Catalytic reaction mechanism of aryl phosphonate under Pd catalysis with high efficiency and broad substrate scopes </details> T he ongoing advancement of phosphorus chemistryremains a topic of enduring significance due to the diverse applications in pharmaceutical science,1 materials chemistry,2 and organic chemistry.3 Introducing phosphorus atoms into organic molecules could result in substantial modifications to their chemical and physical properties, rendering phosphination a commonly employed efficient method for generating innovative compounds. Allenyl phosphine oxides, specific types of P-functionalized unsaturated compounds, have garnered considerable interest in recent years due to their distinctive allenic structure and phosphorus functionality, which embedded them with unique reactive and biological activities.4−7 Therefore, increasing attention has been focusing on the advancement of novel methodologies to acquire phosphorus-substituted allenes. The traditional approach for their preparation mainly relies on the Horner−Mark rearrangement reaction, which underwent an intermediate of propargyl phosphate (Scheme 1a).8 Although delivering the desired allenylphosphoryl compounds, it suffered from toxic and unstable reagents as well as a limited substrate scope. To overcome these issues, transition-metal (TM)-catalyzed coupling of propargylic derivatives with readily available and stable secondary phosphine oxides has been called in for the synthesis of such compounds (Scheme 1b).9 The direct dehydrate C−P coupling of propargylic alcohols is the most straightforward and efficient strategy; however, the C−O bond is much more inert and less reactive. Therefore, Lewis acid catalysts had been applied in such transformations with a high temperature (Scheme 1c).10 Inspired by previous work,11 a catalytic amount of Brønsted acid could facilitate the hydroxy group to form a transient leaving group and could be further converted to construct the C−C bond in the presence of a palladium catalyst.
